title: IKEA's New Saket Store Pairs Swedish Meatballs With Dal Makhani in South Delhi
excerpt: The Swedish retailer opens its second Delhi city store on July 30, with a café menu that blends Nordic staples and Indian comfort food at prices starting at ₹20.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • IKEA's second Delhi store opens on July 30, featuring 30,000 square feet and nearly 3,000 products.
  • The café menu includes Swedish and Indian dishes, with prices starting at ₹20 for soft-serve ice cream.
  • IKEA plans to expand to six stores in Delhi-NCR, focusing on local consumer needs and preferences.
  • The store design reflects insights from home visits, catering to South Delhi's diverse living situations.

From Flat-Pack to Food Court

When IKEA opens the doors of its second Delhi city store at DLF Avenue in Saket on July 30, the Swedish retailer will be selling more than bookshelves and bedframes. The 30,000-square-foot outlet will feature an IKEA Café serving a menu that straddles two culinary worlds: Swedish meatballs alongside paneer butter masala, cinnamon buns next to samosas.

It is a formula IKEA has refined across its Indian stores since entering the market with a Hyderabad outlet in 2018. The food program has become a draw in its own right. At the bistro counter, six samosas go for ₹100, soft-serve vanilla ice cream costs ₹20, and a veg hot dog with mint mayo runs ₹49. In the sit-down restaurant, chicken meatballs are priced at ₹250 for eight pieces or ₹300 for twelve, served with mashed potatoes, vegetables, lingonberry jam, and cream sauce. Indian options include dal makhani at ₹200, paneer butter masala at ₹250, and chicken tikka masala at ₹250.

Designed for South Delhi Living

The Saket store is IKEA's second city-format outlet in Delhi, following the Pacific Mall store in Tagore Garden that opened in West Delhi last year. While smaller than IKEA's sprawling big-box format, the city store carries nearly 3,000 products, with about 1,400 available for immediate purchase. The full IKEA range of more than 6,900 items can be ordered through the website, app, or the company's Shop by Phone service.

"To create an experience that is truly relevant, our teams visited several homes across South Delhi to better understand people's everyday challenges, dreams and aspirations," said Patrik Antoni, CEO of IKEA India. The store's room settings reflect those visits, focusing on adaptable spaces, storage solutions, home offices, guest rooms, balconies, and entertaining areas — the realities of South Delhi's mix of multigenerational houses, builder floors, and compact apartments.

Aggressive Delhi-NCR Expansion

The Saket opening is part of an aggressive push into the Delhi-NCR market, where IKEA says it has more than 300,000 IKEA Family members. The company plans up to six stores in the region, with large-format outlets under development in Noida and Gurgaon. Antoni called Delhi "one of the strongest markets in India" and described the expansion as critical to IKEA's broader India strategy of having at least 30 stores nationwide by 2030.

The approach combines multiple formats: large stores for full immersion, city stores for accessibility, e-commerce for convenience, and Plan and Order Points for services like kitchen and wardrobe design. It is a playbook IKEA has deployed globally, but the Indian execution has required significant localization — from the food menu to the room displays to the product range itself. IKEA currently sources about 30 percent of its products from India and aims to increase that to 50 percent over time.

Where Swedish Meets Desi

For India's middle class, the IKEA Café has become a destination in itself. The ₹20 soft-serve has turned into a social media staple, and the juxtaposition of Swedish meatballs with dal makhani on the same menu captures something about modern Indian consumer culture: global in aspiration, local in taste. The Saket store, positioned in one of South Delhi's premier shopping districts, is a bet that this formula has room to run.
nri_angle: IKEA's fusion of Swedish and Indian food at its Delhi stores mirrors the cultural blending familiar to NRIs, who have long navigated both cuisines in their daily lives abroad.
